title: The Effects of Time Preferences on Cooperation: Experimental Evidence from Infinitely Repeated Games
paper_brief: Lab infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma where all decisions are made at once but stage-game payoffs are spread across weeks or months. Weekly-payment subjects cooperate at 78% in round 1 of the first 10 matches vs 69% for monthly-payment subjects (Table 3, p=0.043); the paper also finds present-bias-reduces-cooperation in a delayed-monthly vs monthly contrast.

title: Expectations-Based Loss Aversion May Help Explain Seemingly Dominated Choices in Strategy-Proof Mechanisms
paper_brief: 72-subject reanalysis of Li (2017a) SP-RSD (Strategy-Proof Random Serial Dictatorship) experimental data testing whether Kőszegi-Rabin (2009) expectations-based reference-dependent (EBRD) preferences with loss aversion can explain seemingly dominated ranking choices in strategy-proof matching mechanisms. Subjects (18 groups of 4) play 10 rounds of RSD, each round allocating 4 prizes drawn from {$0.00, $0.25, $0.50, $0.75, $1.00, $1.25} based on submitted rank-order lists (ROLs) and a private integer priority score 1-10. Dominant strategy is to rank truthfully by value (list '1234'). 720 subject-round observations. Headline descriptive finding (p.541, Section III.C): 29% of submitted ROLs are not 1234 (the truthful dominant-strategy list) — despite RSD being strategy-proof and incentives being clearly explained. 44 of 72 subjects misrepresent in at least one round. Average cost of misrepresentation = $0.21, about 1/3 of the average per-round earning $0.64. Paper's main empirical contribution (Section III.D, Table 4 col 1, p.544): multinomial logit estimate of the EBRD loss-aversion parameter λ = 1.98 (SE 0.18), which is highly statistically significantly different from the classical (no-loss-aversion) benchmark λ=1 — LRT statistic = 32, p < 0.00001, with the observed choices being 'more than 10^7 times likelier with λ = 2 than with λ = 1' (p.521). Robustness: λ = 2.74 (SE 0.31) on the misrepresenters subsample; λ = 3.14 (SE 0.34) on last-5-rounds misrepresenters; λ = 2.2 (SE 0.4) on the one-shot RSD_robustness dataset (stakes 12× higher). Only the SP-RSD treatment is analyzed (fn 7: 'We do not analyze data from Li's (2017a) other DA-related treatment since there, the EBRD model's predictions coincide with those of the classical, reference-independent-preferences model'); the OSP-RSD treatment serves only as a descriptive comparison showing 7% of OSP games end in non-dominant-strategy outcome (fn 24) vs 36% for SP-RSD (main text).

title: Correlation Neglect in Student-to-School Matching
paper_brief: 165-subject within-subject lab experiment (Experiment 1) at Penn State LEMA in Jan-Feb 2019 testing whether the presence of correlation across programs' admissions decisions pushes students' rank-order-list (ROL) submissions toward the aggressive A≻B strategy and away from the diversified A≻C strategy. Each subject completes 9 matched-pair incentivized school-choice scenarios under correlated admissions (common single priority score) and 9 matched-pairs under uncorrelated admissions (independent priorities), yielding 2,970 subject-scenario rows (165 × 18). Headline finding (Section III.D, Figure 1, p.21): aggressive-strategy share is 43.5% under correlated vs 23.4% under uncorrelated — a +20.1-percentage-point gap. Scenario-by-scenario Table 2 (p.20) shows the correlated > uncorrelated aggressive-share pattern holds across all nine scenarios with two-sample difference-of-proportion tests all significant at p<0.05 (seven scenarios at p<0.01). Within-subject preference-reversal rate (choosing A≻B correlated and A≻C uncorrelated) averages 21.1% across scenarios vs 2.9% for the opposite direction (Appendix Table A4). External Enke-Zimmermann correlation-neglect measure χ predicts individual-level preference reversals (Figure 3, Appendix Table A6). Paper also reports Experiment 2 (debiasing interventions in an online sample) and Experiment 3 (structural estimation of χ heterogeneity), but the benchmark curated here is the Experiment 1 PSU-sample aggressive-strategy share gap, which is the paper's headline test.

title: Limited Strategic Thinking and the Cursed Match
paper_brief: 144-subject experiment (48 per treatment × 3 treatments BASE, BEL, COND) at LINEEX Valencia in Dec 2018 testing whether agents anticipate the acceptance curse in vertically differentiated matching markets with private information. BASE: standard 2-player matching game, 3 qualities (H/M/L) × 3 signals (h/m/l); subjects must decide whether to propose a match after observing their own quality and a noisy signal about partner quality. Two reservation-value treatments vary within-subject: Game A (reservation R_M=75, R_H=100) and Game B (reservation R_M=75, R_H=80). Predicted comparative static (Bayesian/cursed): in game A the (H,m) cell should propose strictly less than 50% while (M,m) should propose strictly more; in game B the (H,m) cell should propose more because the lower R_H makes H-types pool with M. Headline (Table 6 p.336, Section III.A Result 2, p.335): the (H,m) proposal rate differs significantly between Games A and B (-0.383 coefficient on H×A interaction, SE 0.065, p<0.01 two-way clustered LPM, N=839) but (M,m) does not (A coefficient -0.008, insignificant) — M-quality subjects fail to respond to the comparative static predicted by acceptance-curse reasoning. BEL and COND robot-protocol treatments then vary scope for belief-formation and conditional-thinking limits (Section IIIB, Tables 7 and 8). Structural QRE estimation (Section IIIC, Table 9) uses data from all three treatments. The curated benchmark is the H×A coefficient from Table 6 (the central formal test of the paper's main hypothesis).

title: Testing Game Theory in the Field: Swedish LUPI Lottery Games
paper_brief: Lab-plus-field study of the Lowest Unique Positive Integer (LUPI) game: players simultaneously pick an integer from 1 to K and whoever picks the lowest number that no one else picked wins a prize. Field data from the Swedish Limbo lottery (49 daily draws, K=99,999) plus lab parallel at CASSEL UCLA (4 sessions, 152 subjects, 49 rounds, K=99, prize $7, 26.9 mean active players per round). Curated benchmark: Table 4 p.25 lab convergence — mean guess in week 1 (rounds 1-7) is 8.56 vs week 7 (rounds 43-49) is 5.84, a 2.72-point drop toward the Poisson-Nash equilibrium average of 5.22 (Python exact 2.740 gap).

title: Equilibrium Selection in the Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma: Axiomatic Approach and Experimental Evidence
paper_brief: Laboratory test of an axiomatic equilibrium-selection criterion for the discounted infinitely repeated symmetric Prisoner's Dilemma. Run at J.W. Goethe University Frankfurt computer lab (May, June, November 2006; 10 sessions × 20 subjects; z-Tree; absolute-stranger matching). Six stage games × three continuation probabilities (δ=0.5, 0.75, 0.875). Each session runs ~19 repeated games (13 for δ=0.875) with a between-treatment stage-game change after RG 11 or RG 8. Curated benchmark: Table 3 p.183 game-3 cooperation rate at δ=0.875 (0.266) minus at δ=0.5 (0.135) = 13.1 pp, a treatment pair where BOTH the standard criterion δ̲ and the axiomatic criterion δ* predict more cooperation under high δ (Class 3 row).

title: Intermediation Reduces Punishment (and Reward)
paper_brief: Harvard Business School CLER laboratory test of whether the presence of a passive intermediary reduces third-party punishment of a selfish first mover. 64 subjects, Aug-Sep 2008, strategy method with 27 scenarios per punisher across 4 repeated rounds. Curated benchmark: Table 1 p.88 Direct minus Sold average punishment pooled across the 6 matched-outcome scenarios (keep $5-$10, intermediary profit = $0) = 2.69 − 2.40 = 0.29. Matches Python replication on 768 subject-scenario rows exactly.

title: Incentive Schemes, Sorting, and Behavioral Biases of Employees: Experimental Evidence
paper_brief: Laboratory experiment testing whether overconfident subjects sort into a convex (nonlinear) incentive scheme over a linear piece-rate. 214 subjects complete a 9-period multiplication real-effort task under No Choice, Choice, or Escalate treatment; in Choice/Escalate, subjects choose between linear and convex schemes each of periods 4-9. Curated benchmark: binary-split nonlinear-choice rate among initially-overconfident subjects (pre-choice belief error > 0 in periods 1-3) minus not-initially-overconfident = 0.595 − 0.571 = 0.025 (Python on subject_rows.jsonl matches old sim_spec). Paper's primary headline coefficient: Table 3 Model 1 overconfidence regression β=0.0184 (p<0.01), implying 23 pp gap between 90th vs 10th percentiles of overconfidence.

title: Local Institutions and the Dynamics of Community Sorting
paper_brief: Tiebout-style community-sorting laboratory experiment testing 4 local public-good institutions (VCM, Ex-Tax, Ex-Provision, Voting). 8 subjects per session (4 High-Type + 4 Low-Type) choose community location and contribute each of 20 periods. Curated benchmark: equal-tax pooled vs VCM share of sorted-segregated subject-periods in final 5 periods = 0.942 − 0.150 = 0.792 (Python exact; paper rounds to 0.79).

title: Separating Bayesian Updating from Non-Probabilistic Reasoning: An Experimental Investigation
paper_brief: Common-value auction experiment comparing auction formats (Active Dutch, Silent Dutch, First-Price Sealed Bid) to isolate Bayesian updating failures vs non-probabilistic reasoning failures. Curated benchmark: Active Dutch minus Silent Dutch winner profit in last 5 epsilon=24 sessions = −2.39 − (−7.06) = 4.67 (Python; paper rounds to 4.66).

title: Pinocchio's Pupil: Using Eyetracking and Pupil Dilation to Understand Truth Telling and Deception in Sender-Receiver Games
paper_brief: Sender-receiver games with eye-tracking and pupil-dilation measurement. Curated benchmark: truthful-message rate at bias=2 (high sender bias) minus bias=0 (no bias) = 0.232 − 0.785 = −0.553. Python exact.

title: Coordination in the Presence of Asset Markets
paper_brief: Lab minimum-input coordination game with an optional asset market on the game's output. Asset markets coordinate players on lower-output, less efficient equilibria. The selected benchmark is the Experiment 1 Figure 1/appendix group-period contrast: Market H Insider mean output 1.1771 versus Control mean output 3.0469, gap -1.8698.

title: Conveniently Upset: Avoiding Altruism by Distorting Beliefs about Others' Altruism
paper_brief: Lab corruption game in which allocators can appropriate tokens from a recipient under a silently-assigned appropriation cap (Able=2 vs Able=8). Curated benchmark: Able=8 − Able=2 tokens taken in the modified-game arm = 5.233 tokens (Table 4, col. 3, p. 3428). Python exact (validated = 5.233397).

title: Obviously Strategy-Proof Mechanisms
paper_brief: Lab auction experiment comparing second-price sealed-bid (strategy-proof) vs ascending-clock (obviously strategy-proof, OSP) formats. In the standard private-value pair, absolute bidding errors are 4.85 units lower under the clock format in rounds 1-5 (Python exact, matches Table 3).

title: Contingent Thinking and the Sure-Thing Principle: Revisiting Classic Anomalies in the Laboratory
paper_brief: Lab voting/contingent-thinking experiment with a 4-round 'AI game' where a robot's type is correlated with the state. In N-correlated rounds the theory-optimal action is Safe; in P-correlated rounds it is Risky. Curated benchmark: Human-Robot arm (treatment==2) N-safe compliance − P-risky compliance = 0.744 − 0.427 = 0.317 (Python exact, matches Table 5 / prose p. 2168).

title: Intrinsic Information Preferences and Skewness
paper_brief: Lab experiment on intrinsic information preferences. Subjects choose whether to acquire informative signals with positively vs negatively skewed structure. Benchmark: positive-skew − negative-skew information-demand share = 0.867 − 0.719 = 0.147 (Python exact).

title: Hindsight, Foresight, and Insight: An Experimental Study of a Small-Market Investment Game with Common and Private Values
paper_brief: Lab small-market endogenous-timing investment game with private cost (3.5/6.5) and binary common-value signal. Subjects play 24 matches and can invest in round 1 or round 2 after seeing the partner's round-1 action. Benchmark: overall investment rate in the Random Two-Cost Treatment (R2CT) = 0.553 after excluding the documented 14-subject pilot, matching the 55 percent printed in Table 4.

title: When Fair Isn't Fair: Understanding Choice Reversals Involving Social Preferences
paper_brief: Lab experiment on surprise-revision fairness task: subjects most often select the ex-ante fair alternative ex-ante, then switch to the ex-post fair alternative ex-post. Benchmark: 71.1% of revisions switch to 50-50 in baseline 4A_4AR treatment (Figure 3).
